questions.q: Which element holds meta-information and is not visible to the user?
options: <body>
<head>
<header>
<html>
questions.concept: head versus header versus body
questions.why: <head> carries meta, title, link and script and renders nothing. <header> is a visible semantic element inside <body>, and <html> is the root element containing both.

questions.q: Which attribute gives the file an element displays?
options: href
alt
src
action
questions.concept: src versus href
questions.why: src names the source file to embed on and

questions.q: Which form attribute gives the URL where the data is sent?
options: method
enctype
target
action
questions.concept: The action attribute of <form>
questions.why: action names the URL, usually a server-side script. method picks GET or POST, enctype matters for file uploads, and target chooses the window.

questions.q: Inside a definition list, which element holds the definition itself?
options: <dd>
<dt>
<td>
<th>
questions.concept: dt is the term, dd is the definition
questions.why: <dl> contains <dt> for the term and <dd> for its definition. <td> and <th> are table data and table header cells inside <tr>.

questions.q: Which form attribute is required when the form handles file uploads?
options: multiple
enctype
pattern
required
questions.concept: enctype="multipart/form-data" for file uploads
questions.why: enctype="multipart/form-data" is needed to handle uploads on the server. multiple allows several selections, pattern sets a regular expression, and required forces a field to be filled.

checks.topic: Sentence structure and function, function versus content words, and concord.

questions.q: Two independent clauses plus at least one dependent clause makes which type?
options: Simple
Complex
Compound-complex
Compound
questions.concept: The clause count that defines compound-complex
questions.why: Compound-complex needs two or more independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. Complex has only one independent clause, compound has no dependent clause, and simple has one clause in total.

questions.q: Which functional type gives commands, instructions or requests?
options: Declarative
Imperative
Interrogative
Exclamatory
questions.concept: Imperative versus declarative
questions.why: An imperative commands, with its subject 'you' understood rather than written. Declarative states information, interrogative asks, and exclamatory expresses strong emotion.

questions.q: Which word class listed below is a function word class?
options: Nouns
Verbs
Adjectives
Pronouns
questions.concept: Function words include pronouns and auxiliaries
questions.why: Function words are conjunctions, auxiliary verbs, prepositions, articles and pronouns. Nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs are the content or lexical words that carry the meaning.

questions.q: Under the Rule of Proximity Agreement, the verb agrees with which subject?
options: The first subject
The closest subject
The plural subject
The longer subject
questions.concept: Proximity agreement with multiple subject elements
questions.why: With several subject elements, especially joined by 'or' or 'nor', the verb aligns with the nearest subject. Plain subject-verb agreement matches the single subject's number instead.

questions.q: In spoken English, which words are stressed or emphasised?
options: Content words
Function words
Articles and prepositions
Auxiliary verbs
questions.concept: The stress test for content versus function words
questions.why: Content words are accentuated while function words remain non-stressed, which is why the distinction aids comprehension and pronunciation. Articles, prepositions and auxiliaries are all function words.

checks.topic: The non-ohmic resistor practical: Ohm's law, Joule's law, the two plots and the procedure.

questions.q: Which plot comes out as a straight line in this experiment?
options: I against V
V against I
P against I²
R against V
questions.concept: Which of the two graphs is straight
questions.why: P against I² is the straight line that verifies Joule's law. I against V is the curve that shows the resistor is non-ohmic, which is the whole point of the experiment.

questions.q: On the P against I² graph, what does the gradient equal?
options: The resistance R
The reciprocal of resistance, 1/R
The current I
The power P
questions.concept: Gradient of P against I² is R
questions.why: Comparing P = R·I² with y = mx + c makes the gradient R, with an intercept of zero. 1/R is the slope of an I against V graph, a different pair of axes.

questions.q: Why is a tungsten filament non-ohmic?
options: Its resistance falls as the current rises
Heating raises its temperature and its resistance
It conducts in one direction only
Its voltage stays constant
questions.concept: Self-heating as the cause of non-linearity
questions.why: Current dissipates heat by P = I²R, the temperature rises and so does R, so the current stops rising linearly. Falling resistance describes a thermistor, and one-way conduction describes a diode.

questions.q: Over which voltage range are readings taken?
options: 0.1 V to 5 V
1 V to 50 V
0.1 V to 50 V
0 V to 100 V
questions.concept: The 0.1 V to 50 V recording range
questions.why: The procedure starts at about 0.1 V and covers the whole available range up to the 50 V limit of the supply, since the curvature only shows at the high-current end.

questions.q: Ohm's law requires the resistance to be independent of what?
options: The magnitude and polarity of the applied p.d.
The room temperature
The length of the conductor
The meter used to read it
questions.concept: The lab statement of Ohm's law
questions.why: A device is ohmic if resistance between two points is independent of the magnitude and polarity of the potential difference, which is why a diode counts as non-ohmic even though each branch looks straight.

recapCandidates.topic: The limit of f at a is decided entirely by the values of f at points near a and never by f(a) itself. That is why (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) has the limit 4 at x = 2 even though the function has no value there, and it is the reason cancelling the factor (x - 2) is legitimate rather than a fudge.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students read lim(x to a) f(x) as an instruction to substitute a into f, so they treat the limit as a slow way of computing f(a); the model survives because for polynomials and for rational functions with a non-zero denominator the two really do coincide, and those are most of the examples they meet, so it only breaks at exactly the holes, jumps and 0/0 forms the topic exists to handle.
whyQuestions: Why does the definition insist on 0 < |x - a| rather than just |x - a| < delta?
Why can (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) have a limit of 4 at x = 2 when the function has no value at x = 2?
Why is cancelling the factor (x - 2) legitimate here, when that factor is zero at the very point we are heading towards?
Why does continuity have to be stated as a separate three-part condition instead of following automatically from the limit existing?
Why does this same idea explain what is going on when L'Hopital's Rule is applied to a 0/0 quotient?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
It states the punctured-neighbourhood point explicitly: the definition constrains only x with 0 < |x - a| < delta, so f(a) is never consulted and can be changed, or left undefined, without altering the limit.
It uses that to justify cancellation: the reduced function agrees with the original at every x except a, and since limits never look at a, the two functions must have the same limit there.
It separates limit from value with a concrete case of each kind: a hole where the limit exists but f(a) does not, and a jump such as |x|/x at 0 where the one-sided limits disagree so no limit exists at all, and it names continuity as the extra demand that f(a) exists and equals the limit.
recapCandidates.workedExample: Evaluate lim(x to 2) (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2). Step 1, substitute: (4 - 4)/(2 - 2) = 0/0, indeterminate, so substitution is not available and the point x = 2 is not in the domain. Step 2, factor the numerator as a difference of squares: x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2). Step 3, cancel: for every x not equal to 2 the quotient (x - 2)(x + 2)/(x - 2) equals x + 2; the cancellation is valid precisely because the limit process only uses x not equal to 2, where (x - 2)/(x - 2) is genuinely 1. Step 4, the reduced function x + 2 is a polynomial, hence continuous, so lim(x to 2) (x + 2) = 4. Therefore the limit is 4. Step 5, interpret: f(2) does not exist, so f is not continuous at 2, but the limit does exist, so the discontinuity is removable; defining f(2) = 4 patches the hole and makes f continuous. Cross-check with L'Hopital: differentiating numerator and denominator separately gives 2x/1, which at x = 2 is 4, the same answer, and for the same reason, namely that both routes strip out the common vanishing factor (x - 2).

recapCandidates.topic: A cell's emf is a fixed property of its chemistry, but the voltage you can measure across its terminals is not: as soon as current flows, a p.d. of Ir is dropped across the cell's own internal resistance and is dissipated inside the cell, so V = epsilon - Ir. Emf is energy supplied per coulomb, and only the part left after the internal loss is delivered to the external circuit.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Students treat 'the emf' and 'the battery's voltage' as the same number and solve loops with I = epsilon/R; this survives because in most textbook and lab circuits the external resistance is far larger than r, so V is within a per cent of epsilon and the wrong method still gives nearly the right answer — it only breaks visibly at high current, near short circuit, or in the V-I graph experiment where the whole point is the slope.
whyQuestions: Why is emf measured in volts and not in newtons, if it is called a force?
Why does a voltmeter read 1.5 V across an idle torch cell but only 1.2 V once the bulb is lit?
Why does the loop equation use R + r rather than R alone, when the resistor is the only thing you can see?
Why is the gradient of the V against I graph equal to minus r, and why is the intercept, not the gradient, the emf?
Why does a nearly short-circuited cell get hot while delivering almost no useful power to the external circuit?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
Emf is defined as work done per unit charge, epsilon = W/Q, so its unit is the volt (joule per coulomb) and its dimension is M L^2 T^-3 I^-1; it is a property of the source, fixed by its chemistry.
The current in a single loop is the same everywhere, so the emf is shared between the external drop and the internal drop: epsilon = IR + Ir = I(R + r), which rearranges to V = epsilon - Ir; the lost volts Ir are dissipated as heat inside the cell.
The measurement follows from this: V = epsilon - rI is a straight line of gradient -r with V-axis intercept epsilon, so extrapolating to zero current is the only condition under which terminal p.d. and emf coincide.
recapCandidates.workedExample:
A cell of emf 1.50 V and internal resistance 0.50 ohm is connected first to R = 2.5 ohm and then to R = 0.10 ohm.
Case 1: I = epsilon/(R + r) = 1.50/(2.5 + 0.50) = 0.50 A. Terminal p.d. V = epsilon - Ir = 1.50 - 0.50 x 0.50 = 1.25 V, and as a check V = IR = 0.50 x 2.5 = 1.25 V. Power to the load = I^2 R = 0.625 W; power wasted inside = I^2 r = 0.125 W.
Case 2: I = 1.50/(0.10 + 0.50) = 2.5 A. V = 1.50 - 2.5 x 0.50 = 0.25 V. Power to the load = I^2 R = 0.625 W, but power wasted inside = I^2 r = 3.13 W — five times more heat in the cell than useful output.
Moral: the same cell, same emf, delivers 1.25 V or 0.25 V depending only on the load, and the naive I = epsilon/R would have predicted 0.60 A and 15 A respectively. Reading the graph back: plotting the two points (0.50 A, 1.25 V) and (2.5 A, 0.25 V) gives gradient (0.25 - 1.25)/(2.5 - 0.50) = -0.50 V/A, so r = 0.50 ohm, and the intercept at I = 0 is 1.50 V, the emf.
